title: Room and Smile
premise: Ada Nystrom, a pest controller who has spent two decades hiding behind rational explanations, is called to the village of Hollowmere where something leaves human fingerprints in flour dust and ash. The village's church bell—melted down in 1911—rings each dusk, and Ada realizes the sound is a summons tied to an object stolen from the church in 1974: a silver reliquary her own mother helped take. As the harvest moon approaches, the villagers' faces begin to change into versions of people who vanished decades ago, and Ada's carefully constructed identity as an outsider dissolves. In the climax beneath the ruined bell tower, Ada returns the reliquary and offers the one thing she has never given anyone—her true name—and the entity, finally seen, releases the village; Ada stays, no longer invisible but belonging at last.
about_author: Isandro Dravenmoor is the pen name of a former rural surveyor who spent years documenting abandoned churches across northern England before turning to horror fiction. They write in a converted chapel, insisting that the drafts are better since 'the tenant' moved in.

chapters.title: The Callout
chapters.summary: Third-person limited on Ada Nystrom, who takes a pest-control job in Hollowmere after her usual contracts dry up. The client, Mrs. Ellery, insists the problem isn't rats—it's 'the visitor.' Ada finds small handprints in flour dust, five fingers, too precise for animals. Emotional beat: professional detachment masking old unease.

chapters.title: Fingerprints
chapters.summary: Ada's POV. She sets traps and dusts surfaces, cataloguing evidence like a scientist. The prints appear inside sealed cupboards and on the ceiling, always at shoulder height of a standing adult. A neighbor watches her house all night without blinking. Beat: Ada's rationalism begins to cost her sleep.

chapters.title: A Bell That Isn't There
chapters.summary: At dusk the church bell rings, though the tower is empty—the bell was melted down in 1911. Ada interviews the vicar, Mr. Tallow, who smiles too long and says 'it rings for whoever owes it.' Beat: first crack in Ada's explanatory framework.

chapters.title: Twenty Years of Explanations
chapters.summary: Flashback chapter in Ada's POV: childhood in a farmhouse with noises in the walls, a mother who hummed to them like they were pets. Ada learned to rename every fear until fear went quiet. Present-day Ada wakes to find the word ADA written in flour on her van window. Beat: the past refuses renaming.

chapters.title: The Village That Looks Back
chapters.summary: Ada canvasses Hollowmere for sightings. Villagers are courteous but identical in their courtesy, as if rehearsed. An old woman, Grete, grips her wrist: 'You have her chin. Come back before the moon fattens.' Beat: Ada realizes she's recognized, not anonymous.

chapters.title: Parish Records
chapters.summary: In the archive, Ada finds the 1974 theft report: a silver reliquary taken from the church, suspects never named. A grainy photo shows three young women—one is unmistakably her mother. Beat: dread becomes personal inheritance.

chapters.title: What Mother Took
chapters.summary: Ada calls her estranged mother, now in a care home, who mistakes her for someone named Liss and whispers, 'We only borrowed it. It said we could give it back whenever.' Line goes dead mid-sentence. Beat: guilt surfacing through dementia's fog.

chapters.title: The Visitor's Shape
chapters.summary: Night stakeout in Mrs. Ellery's kitchen. Ada sees it: a figure made of gathered dark, wearing the posture of a person waiting politely. It presses its palm to the window—leaving a print—and mouths something. She reads the shape of her own name. Beat: terror fused with terrible intimacy.

chapters.title: Faces Changing
chapters.summary: Villagers begin resembling the missing: the postman has a drowned man's eyes; children recite names from 1953. Tallow leads dusk services facing the empty tower. Ada photographs everything; the photos show only smiling villagers. Beat: reality's documentation fails.

chapters.title: Grete's Testimony
chapters.summary: Grete, lucid for once, recounts 1974: three girls took the reliquary as a dare, and the bell began ringing that same night. One girl stayed in Hollowmere forever. One left and was followed by silence all her life. The third became Ada's mother. Beat: Ada learns the debt is hers to pay.

chapters.title: The Care Home
chapters.summary: Ada visits her mother, who surfaces briefly and begs her not to return what they took—'It wants a name, Ada, it will take yours.' She presses a key into Ada's hand: the old farmhouse. Beat: love expressed as warning, deepening Ada's conflict between loyalty and duty.

chapters.title: The Farmhouse Key
chapters.summary: Ada returns to her childhood home, unchanged for twenty years, dust undisturbed except fresh prints leading upstairs. In the attic, under floorboards, she finds the reliquary wrapped in her baby blanket. It is warm. Beat: the object has been waiting for her specifically.

chapters.title: Belonging Offered
chapters.summary: That night the visitor sits in Ada's kitchen chair, patient. It doesn't threaten; it offers—a place at the table, a seat in the village, an end to invisibility. Ada, starving for belonging, nearly says yes. Beat: temptation articulated as kindness, the theme of power's corruption inverted.

chapters.title: Tallow's Bargain
chapters.summary: Vicar Tallow reveals the village's arrangement: each generation gives the entity one name to keep the rest safe. He offers to substitute Ada's name for his own dying congregation's—if she simply stays and lets herself be claimed. Beat: institutional evil dressed as mercy.

chapters.title: The Harvest Moon Rises
chapters.summary: Two nights remain. Ada researches the reliquary: it once held the parish's founding covenant, a list of every villager's true name. Whoever holds it holds the village's identity. The entity cannot take what is freely returned. Beat: stakes crystallize; plan forms.

chapters.title: They Know My Name
chapters.summary: Hollowmere turns on Ada gently—doors open before she knocks, everyone greets her by a childhood nickname only her mother used. Her reflection lags half a second. She is being absorbed already. Beat: identity erosion, isolation even among the welcoming.

chapters.title: Liss
chapters.summary: Ada discovers who Liss was: the third girl, her mother's sister, who stayed in Hollowmere in 1974 and became the entity's first kept name. The visitor wears Liss's shape because it keeps what it's given. Beat: grief reframes the monster as a hoarder of the surrendered.

chapters.title: The Bell Tower
chapters.summary: Harvest moon night. Ada climbs the empty tower with the reliquary as the whole village gathers below, faces tilted, smiling in unison. The bell rings from nothing, each toll peeling away a memory of her own name. Beat: ascent toward sacrifice, tension at maximum.

chapters.title: Return What Was Taken
chapters.summary: At the top, Ada opens the reliquary: the covenant pages are blank except for three names—hers, her mother's, Liss's. She speaks her full true name aloud and places the reliquary in the air where the bell hung. The entity arrives, vast and patient, and accepts. Beat: climax; surrender transformed into gift.

chapters.title: One Toll
chapters.summary: The bell rings once, solid and real, then falls silent forever. The villagers collapse into themselves, weeping, their own faces returning. Liss's shape steps out of the entity's mass—an old woman now—and thanks Ada before dissolving into dawn light. Beat: release and mourning entwined.

chapters.title: Aftermath
chapters.summary: Weeks later, Hollowmere is ordinary and slightly embarrassed. Tallow resigns; Grete plants marigolds. Ada's mother, briefly lucid, remembers giving her the key and says, 'You came back. That was the payment all along.' Beat: tenderness after horror; belonging earned, not claimed.

chapters.title: Room and Smile
chapters.summary: Ada stays in Hollowmere, keeping the pest-control rounds, no longer invisible—greeted by name, invited to tables. On quiet evenings she hears nothing in the walls, and one night, faintly, what might be a smile in the dark that does not ask for anything. Final beat: peace with a held breath; belonging chosen, watched, and warm.
